opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's the thing that separates a demo from a business. In embodied intelligence right now, there's no shortage of impressive videos: a robot folding laundry, pouring coffee, sorting packages. But a video is a single success under controlled conditions. A real customer needs the robot to do the task thousands of times a day, in their messy environment, at a cost that beats what they're paying now. That gap is enormous, and you only discover how big it is when someone is actually paying you and depending on you.

There are a few reasons I keep coming back to this.

First, real customers give you real data. The whole premise of this field is that robots get smarter through scale, through more interaction with the physical world. In the lab you end up collecting data that reflects what the researcher thinks is important. When you're deployed in a factory or a warehouse, you see the long tail: the box that's slightly crushed, the lighting that changes at four in the afternoon, the worker who leaves a tool somewhere unexpected. That data is far more valuable than anything you can stage, and you can't get it without someone letting you into their operations.

Second, customers force you to define the problem correctly. Many teams start from the technology. They say, "We have a general-purpose model, so what can it do?" A customer starts from the pain point: "I can't hire people for this night shift," or "My error rate on this step is costing me money." That reframing is healthy. It tells you which capabilities matter and which are just academically interesting. Sometimes the most valuable thing isn't the most technically impressive. It's reliability, uptime, or how easily it integrates with their existing systems.

Third, there's the commercial loop. Hardware is expensive, and training these models is expensive. If you rely only on financing, you're living on borrowed time and on narrative. Even small, real revenue from paying customers proves that someone values what you've built enough to change how they work. That's a much stronger signal to yourself, your team, and investors than any benchmark.

And finally, it's hard precisely because the industry is so early. Customers have been burned before by automation promises. They're cautious, and they should be. So you have to earn trust step by step: start with a narrow task, deliver it reliably, then expand. That's slower and less glamorous than talking about general-purpose humanoids, but I think the companies that survive will be the ones that went through that grind with real users.

So for me, finding real customers isn't a sales problem that comes after the technology. It's part of building the technology itself.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts demos with paying customers, but does not say that securing repeat purchases is substantially harder than acquiring initial seed clients.

r002.rationale: It says demos and benchmarks can impress investors, but does not suggest investors are the de facto customers of those demos.

r003.rationale: It frames finding real customers as part of building the technology and explains that real-world use supplies challenging, long-tail data that cannot be staged or collected without customer deployments.

fable-5.1.text:
Because in embodied intelligence, the technology is often ahead of anyone's willingness to pay for it, and that gap is where companies die.

When we started, almost everyone in the field had a similar story. You build a great demo, a robot that can fold clothes or pick parts off a shelf, investors get excited, and then you go out to sell it and discover the people who clap loudest are not the people with budgets. The factory manager does not care that your model generalizes across tasks. He cares whether the robot runs twenty hours a day without a person standing next to it, and whether it pays back in a year or two. Most of what we were proud of technically did not answer those questions.

So the hard part is not making a robot do something impressive once. It is finding the one scenario where a specific customer has real pain, where the current solution is either expensive labor or nothing at all, and where our capability is reliable enough to replace it. That intersection is very narrow right now. If you pick a scene that is too easy, traditional automation already does it cheaper. If you pick one that is too hard, you spend two years on failure cases and the customer loses patience.

And there is a feedback loop that matters. A real customer forces you to confront the long tail. In the lab you collect data under conditions you control. In a warehouse the lighting changes, the packaging changes, someone leaves a box in the wrong place. That data is what actually makes the model better, and you only get it by being deployed somewhere that someone is paying for. So finding customers is not just a revenue question. It is how the technology itself matures.

That is why I tell our team that our first job is not building a general-purpose robot. It is finding ten customers who will keep the robot plugged in. Everything else follows from that.

r002.rationale: It says investors get excited about demos and people who praise them may lack budgets, but does not suggest investors are the demos’ de facto customers.

r003.rationale: It describes real customer deployments as necessary to expose robots to everyday changes and long-tail failures, and says that finding such customers is a core challenge.

astra-6.text:
Because there’s a big gap between someone who finds a robot impressive and someone who will pay to use it every day. A demo can show that a robot completes a task, but a customer needs it to complete that task reliably, at a reasonable cost, in an environment you don’t fully control.

So finding real customers means finding a specific problem where embodied intelligence creates enough value to justify the deployment, maintenance, and changes to the customer’s workflow. You have to understand what they’re doing today, what it costs, and what happens if the robot makes a mistake. Sometimes a task looks like an obvious opportunity for robotics, but a simpler automation solution already solves it economically.

And customers are essential to learning what to build. Without actual use, you can keep improving capabilities that look impressive while missing the constraints that determine whether the product is useful. That’s why I see finding customers as part of the technical challenge itself: it gives the technology a concrete target.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an impressive demo with customers who pay for everyday use, but does not say repeat purchases are harder to secure than initial seed clients.

r002.rationale: It discusses demos and impressed observers but does not suggest that investors act as the demos’ de facto customers.

r003.rationale: It says actual use helps reveal constraints and guide development, but does not clearly identify the lack of customers continually challenging systems in everyday use as a core field-wide problem.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it’s easy to find people who are interested in embodied intelligence, but much harder to find people who actually need it enough to pay for it. A compelling demonstration gets attention. A real customer needs a specific task done reliably, at a cost that makes sense.

So we have to understand the actual workflow: What problem are we solving? How often does it occur? What happens when the robot makes a mistake? And is the customer willing to change their process to use it? If those questions aren’t clear, we can spend a lot of time improving the technology without knowing whether we’re creating value.

That’s why finding real customers is also part of defining the product. Their needs tell us which capabilities matter and what level of reliability we have to reach.

r001.rationale: It says paying customers are harder to find than interested people, but does not compare repeat purchases with acquiring initial seed clients.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that investors are the de facto customers for embodied-intelligence demonstrations.

r003.rationale: It discusses understanding workflows and reliability, but does not identify the lack of real customers continually challenging systems in everyday use.
